newsitem.title: USA: Health groups urge states to insure more children.
newsitem.headline: Health groups urge states to insure more children.

text.p: The number of children lacking health insurance in the South has been reduced but state Medicaid programs should expand to cover some four million who still lack it, health advocacy groups said Monday.

The number of uninsured children in the South declined from 1989-93 but a disproportionate number of uninsured children still live in those 17 states plus Washington, D.C., according to the study by the Southern Institute on Children and Families and sponsored by the Kaiser Family Foundation.

Just over one third of American children -- 36 percent -- live in the South but 43 percent of the nation's uninsured children live there, the study said. Of the estimated 9.4 million uninsured children in the United States, about four million live in the South.
Older children from ages 13 to 18 are a bigger uninsured problem than those under age 5 because states have broadened Medicaid eligibility for the younger children, it said.

In addition, changes in state welfare programs and rules governing eligibility for programs for the disabled may erode some of the progress in expanding health coverage for children, Sarah Shuptine, president of the Southern Institute, said. She said states have the flexibility to broaden many aspects of Medicaid without seeking federal waivers or waiting for nationwide reform to be approved by Congress.
The Kaiser Foundation has estimated it costs about $1,200 per year for each child added to Medicaid.

Congress last year debated replacing the current state-federal Medicaid program with block grants to states. It was unclear what type of Medicaid reforms Congress will seek to enact next year or how much money they will seek to save from the program.
Some Democrats, in the minority in Congress, were advocating expanding children's coverage.
